notes:
- **Phone, drone and camera DNGs straighten their own lenses.** Many phones and drones, and some cameras (Google Pixel, DJI, Leica, GoPro and others), write a correction for their own lens's distortion into the DNG file, and wide lenses there can bow a horizon or leave the frame's corners dark without it. A photograph that carries one now starts with it on the first time you open it, in the Lens section, where the profile line reads **Profile: from the file** and you can switch it off like any other edit. It takes the place of a database profile, so the lens is never corrected twice; photographs you already edited keep their look, and **Apply** puts the file's correction on them. [Lens](https://www.heeler.app/docs/adjustments/lens/#profiles).
- **Presets are files you can read and edit.** Saved and exported presets are now written in YAML, the same format as node recipe files: each node's settings on its own line, in plain words, editable in any text editor, with any mistake reported by its line. Presets saved or shared from earlier versions are JSON and still import and apply as before; Heeler writes them as YAML the next time it saves or exports them. [Presets](https://www.heeler.app/docs/presets/#preset-files).
- **Phone, drone and GoPro raw files have even corners.** Many phones (iPhone, Google Pixel, ASUS and other Android phones), DJI drones and the Hasselblad cameras on DJI drones, and every GoPro write a lens shading correction into their raw files, which the reader is meant to apply: it brightens the corners the lens leaves dark, and evens out any color shift there. Heeler now applies it, so these photographs develop with even light across the frame instead of dark, sometimes tinted, corners; on a Pixel 3a or an iPhone 7 Plus the corners come out two to three times brighter. A photograph you already edited keeps its edits, but its corners change. A Vignette added to make up for the dark corners may no longer be needed. [Library](https://www.heeler.app/docs/library/).
- **Fujifilm X-Trans photographs develop three to four times faster.** The full-size develop of an X-Trans file, the slowest step in opening one, now shares its work between up to four of your computer's cores: a 40 megapixel X-T50 frame takes about 4 seconds instead of 13, and an X-H2 frame about 5 instead of 24. The picture is the same, apart from a few pixels along the seams where the develop splits its work, which now come out the way every other pixel does.
- **Faster TIFF, JPEG and PNG exports.** Turning the finished picture into a 16-bit TIFF now uses all your cores, and takes about an eighth of the time it did; JPEG and PNG exports are about 30% faster. The files are exactly the same as before.
- **Lens corrections stay on the lens when you crop.** The Lens section's correction ran after Crop & Rotate, so once a photograph was cropped, straightened, rotated or flipped, a lens profile was centered on the cropped frame and scaled to it rather than to the lens. The lens correction now runs first, on the whole frame the camera recorded. Photographs you already edited are moved to the new order when you open them; one with both a lens correction and a crop can change slightly toward its edges, where the correction is now the one its lens needs. [Lens](https://www.heeler.app/docs/adjustments/lens/).
- **Long edits preview in less memory.** While the preview redrew a photograph with a long chain of edits, it held on to every step's picture until the frame was done, so a big graph could use far more memory than Heeler had set aside and slow the whole computer down. It now lets go of each step's picture once nothing later in the frame needs it, and keeps only what it will reuse for the next frame.
- **The right size for Nikon and many other raw files from the start.** Before a photograph's first full develop, Heeler reads its size from the file, and for about a third of raw files (most Nikon NEFs, many DNGs and Fujifilm RAFs, every Canon CRW and Phase One IIQ) it read the small preview's size instead: a Nikon D200 frame as 160 by 120. Clicking 100% could land at the wrong scale, and a pixel-sized setting such as a Blur radius could look stronger in the preview than in the export until the develop finished. The size now comes from the raw data itself, and a library that already recorded a wrong size is corrected the next time the photograph develops.
- **Raw files saved as .TIF open as the photograph.** Older Kodak DCS cameras, Canon's EOS-1D, EOS-1Ds and D2000, and Phase One backs saved their raw files with a .TIF name. Heeler opened them as ordinary TIFFs and showed only the small preview stored at the start of the file, as little as 156 by 104 pixels. They now develop like any other raw file, at full size, in the library and the editor. Ordinary TIFFs, including Heeler's own exports, open as before. [Library](https://www.heeler.app/docs/library/).
